localBiteReport: The most current reports available for Choctawhatchee Bay are from late July/early August 2026, with the most recent individual charter post dated approximately July 27 (about 6 days ago). Speckled trout are the dominant inshore story right now — guides report trout scattered throughout the bay and still feeding actively despite windy conditions, with anglers advised to be selective about where they fish until the wind settles. Bull redfish are also in the mix and receiving a lot of attention; one recent trip landed a 40¼-inch, 26-lb bull red, and limit catches of upper-slot reds have been reported out of Santa Rosa Beach. A late-June trip on West Bay/Choctawhatchee also produced speckled trout, slot reds, and a notable 43-lb black drum, suggesting black drum remain a legitimate target around the bay system. Water temperature at this location is 85°F. Note: the Half Hitch Destin fishing report blog appears to have last posted on June 15, 2026 — no July update was findable — so that source is not reflected here.

aiSummary: Speckled trout and bull redfish are the dominant inshore story on Choctawhatchee Bay right now, with guides reporting trout scattered throughout the bay and actively feeding, and bull reds drawing serious attention — including a recent 40¼-inch, 26-lb fish. Today's forecast throws a significant wrench into plans: an 88% storm chance with the active window before 4 PM means open, exposed water should be avoided or wrapped up early, and protected bayous on both sides of the bay are the smart play. Water temps are sitting at 85°F with slightly stained clarity, so slow down presentations and focus on structure and shade wherever you fish.

bridge.aiNote: The 331 Bridge spans the narrow neck of Choctawhatchee Bay, creating a current funnel where bait gets pushed through on both tides. Pilings hold speckled trout, redfish, sheepshead, and black drum year-round, with the lee-side pilings serving as the prime ambush zone on incoming tides. That said, the open water here is fully exposed to weather and chop — it's typically the first spot on the bay to become unfishable when wind picks up.
bridge.todaysCall: Today is a tough draw for the 331 Bridge. WSW winds at 10–15 mph will push chop directly into the open channel, and with an 88% storm chance before 4 PM you'd have a very narrow safe window. If you go, be on the water at or just after the 9:14 AM high tide when current transitions and bait stacks against the pilings — work the lee-side structure fast and get off the water well before noon. The waning gibbous moon is providing a moderate tidal push that should move bait through the funnel, which is a plus for the bite. Honestly, unless you can fish the early morning window and commit to being off the water by 11 AM, a protected bayou is the safer and smarter call today.

alaqua.aiNote: Alaqua Bayou offers some of the most reliably protected water on the north side of Choctawhatchee Bay, with a strong year-round redfish population and trout and flounder showing at the mouth. The oyster bars at the creek mouth are the prime target, and tree cover keeps interior water a few degrees cooler than the open bay while also providing meaningful shelter from wind and weather. The upper creek transitions toward brackish water and can hold bass alongside smaller reds.
alaqua.todaysCall: Alaqua Bayou is one of the better calls on a day like today — the tree cover and creek orientation will knock down the WSW wind significantly, and the protected character makes it a reasonable place to fish through the morning before the storm window opens up. Focus on the oyster bars at the mouth during the outgoing tide that sets up after the 9:14 AM high; slightly stained water at 85°F means reds will be using structure and shade rather than cruising open flats. The bay-wide redfish bite has been strong, including limit catches of upper-slot fish, so this spot's year-round red population should be active. Just watch the sky closely — with storms likely before 4 PM, plan to be off the water no later than early afternoon.

basin.aiNote: Basin Bayou sees less fishing pressure than nearby Alaqua or LaGrange, which tends to translate into less-educated fish and a more relaxed bite. The interior grass flats are classic sight-fishing territory for redfish in under two feet of water, and pompano occasionally show at the mouth on moving tides in late spring and early summer. It is notably less protected than LaGrange when weather builds, which is worth factoring into any trip decision.
basin.todaysCall: Basin Bayou's lower pressure is an asset today — if you can get in there during the morning hours, reds on the interior grass flats may be less finicky than fish in spots that see more boat traffic. The outgoing tide after the 9:14 AM high will begin pushing water off those shallow flats, which is often when redfish get active and feedable along the edges. Slightly stained water actually helps your approach on those skinny-water flats by masking your presence a bit. However, Basin offers less weather protection than LaGrange, so if the storm threat materializes early, you'll want an exit plan — commit to fishing the morning window and be ready to run before things build.

lagrange.aiNote: LaGrange Bayou is consistently the top trout producer in this bay system, with legendary oyster bars at the mouth and interior grass flats that hold redfish year-round. Deep holes inside the bayou hold black drum and sheepshead, and the habitat diversity makes it productive across multiple species and tide stages. It is also the most protected water on the north side of the bay, making it the go-to refuge when weather builds — a key attribute in summer.
lagrange.todaysCall: LaGrange is the right call today, full stop. The combination of maximum weather protection, top-tier trout and redfish habitat, and a live bay-wide bite report that includes both speckled trout scattered throughout the system and bull redfish actively feeding makes this the safest and most productive option under an 88% storm chance. Fish the oyster bars at the mouth hard on the outgoing tide that follows the 9:14 AM high — slightly stained water keeps fish tucked tighter to structure, so put your bait right on the shell. The waning gibbous moon is providing a moderate tidal push that should flush bait through the mouth nicely. If the black drum reports from West Bay/Choctawhatchee in late June translate here, the deep interior holes are worth a slow-rolled crab or cut bait before you leave.

fourmile.aiNote: Four Mile Creek is a short tidal creek running between Shipyard Marina and Choctawhatchee Bay, with tidal flow that pushes baitfish up the creek on incoming tides and concentrates reds and trout in the bends and along grass edges. The creek mouth is a reliable flounder zone, and the upper section transitions toward brackish water where bass mix with smaller reds. Its short length and creek character make it one of the safest and most manageable fisheries on the bay when weather threatens.
fourmile.todaysCall: Four Mile Creek is a legitimate storm-day option — it's short, sheltered, and close to the ramp, meaning you can fish confidently and bail quickly if conditions deteriorate. The tide is outgoing after 9:14 AM, which will push baitfish toward the mouth and concentrate reds and trout in the lower bends and grass edges — that's your primary window. Water temp is 85°F and clarity is slightly stained, so work slower presentations tight to any shaded bank or grass edge you can find. The bay-wide trout bite is active right now, so don't overlook the trout pattern here even if reds are the marquee species. Be off the water by early afternoon with an 88% storm chance in play.

hogtown.aiNote: Hogtown Bayou is a signature Santa Rosa Beach guide spot and one of the most consistently productive trout flats on the bay, with summer mornings being peak time as trout stack on grass in two to four feet of water. Spanish mackerel also show at the mouth on moving tides, adding a bonus species to the program. It sees regular pressure but continues to produce reliably, though anglers should factor in the longer run time compared to bayous closer to the 331 Bridge.
hogtown.todaysCall: Hogtown Bayou is worth the run today if you get out early — the bay-wide trout bite is firmly on, and guides have specifically flagged the Santa Rosa Beach area as productive for upper-slot reds recently, which aligns with Hogtown's location. Target the grass flats in two to four feet of water during the early morning hours before the tide fully turns at 9:14 AM, then continue working the flats on the early outgoing. WSW winds at 10–15 mph are workable inside the bayou but will make the run from the north-side ramps rougher than ideal, so factor that into your departure time. With an 88% storm chance before 4 PM, the longer run distance is the real concern — build in extra buffer time and be back at the dock no later than midday. Do not push your luck on the return run if you see cells building to the west.

mallet.aiNote: Mallet Bayou is a small tributary that feeds directly into LaGrange Bayou just south of Freeport, and that direct connection means LaGrange's well-documented oyster-bar trout-and-redfish pattern plausibly extends into this quieter, smaller water. There is considerably less documented fishing history for Mallet Bayou itself compared to its larger neighbor, but its small and interior character makes it a logical calm-water fallback when wind builds on the open bay. Think of it as a quieter extension of the LaGrange complex rather than a standalone destination.
mallet.todaysCall: If LaGrange Bayou's main oyster bars get crowded — which is plausible on a day when everyone is seeking protected water — Mallet Bayou offers a quieter, less pressured alternative within the same connected system. The outgoing tide after the 9:14 AM high should push water and bait through both bayous similarly, so the same trout-on-structure, reds-on-grass pattern that works in LaGrange should translate here. Slightly stained water and 85°F temps mean fish will be holding tight — work any visible oyster structure or grass edge slowly. Because it's small and interior, it's one of the safest places on the bay to wait out a developing storm situation, but have your exit back to the ramp mentally mapped before conditions change.

mack.aiNote: Mack Bayou sits on the barrier-island (30-A) side of Choctawhatchee Bay near Topsail Hill Preserve State Park, well west of the 331 Bridge — this is a long-run destination, not a quick local trip. It shares the same protected-bayou character as Alaqua and LaGrange, with marsh grass, oyster bars, and interior holes, and it sees less pressure than north-side spots simply because of the distance involved. Hewett and Buck Bayou sit immediately to the east and are realistically fishable in the same outing.
mack.todaysCall: The long run to Mack Bayou is the central issue today — with an 88% storm chance and the active window before 4 PM, committing to a distant destination on the 30-A side significantly compresses your safety margin for the return trip. If you're already based near Santa Rosa Beach or launching from the south side, the calculus changes, and the light pressure and protected habitat here make it a genuinely attractive option. Fish the oyster bars and marsh grass edges on the outgoing tide after 9:14 AM; slightly stained water at 85°F is well-suited to slow, bottom-oriented presentations for reds. Combine with Hewett Bayou to make the run worthwhile, but commit to a hard turnaround time of no later than early afternoon given today's forecast.

hewett.aiNote: Hewett Bayou sits immediately east of Mack Bayou on the barrier-island (30-A) side of Choctawhatchee Bay, near Topsail Hill Preserve State Park, and pairs naturally with Mack and Buck Bayou in a single trip. It offers the same protected-bayou habitat as its neighbors — oyster bars and marsh grass at the mouth, with deeper interior holes further in — and sees light pressure due to its distance from the main boat ramps. Like Mack Bayou, it is a long-run destination from the 331 Bridge area.
hewett.todaysCall: Hewett Bayou makes the most sense today as part of a Mack-and-Hewett combo rather than a solo destination, both to justify the run and to give you options if one spot is slow. The protected habitat and light pressure are genuine assets on a day when every angler on the bay is likely funneling into the same few sheltered spots closer to the bridge. Work the oyster bar and marsh grass structure on the outgoing tide after 9:14 AM with the same slow, stained-water approach you'd use anywhere on the bay today. The same caution applies as for Mack — the long run back in building afternoon weather is the real risk factor, so set a firm off-the-water time before you leave the ramp and stick to it.

buck.aiNote: Buck Bayou is the smallest and least-documented of the three neighboring bayous on the barrier-island (30-A) side of Choctawhatchee Bay, near Topsail Hill Preserve State Park. Its habitat should track its larger neighbors — marsh grass, some oyster structure, and a modest interior — but there is less basis to speak confidently about its fishing compared to Mack or Hewett. It is best treated as a bonus stop on a Mack and Hewett Bayou trip rather than a standalone destination.
buck.todaysCall: Buck Bayou is worth a look only if you're already running the Mack-Hewett corridor today — treat it as a 20-minute bonus stop rather than a reason to make the run in its own right. If the other two bayous are producing on the outgoing tide, Buck's similar habitat should be in play for the same redfish and trout pattern; if they're slow, don't burn extra time here. Given today's storm threat, use Buck early in the outing rather than as a late stop — you don't want to be in your farthest, smallest, least-familiar water when a cell starts building. The same hard turnaround rule applies: be heading back well before early afternoon.
